records.text: One piece, several targets, all hit at once. That's a fork, and it's my favorite kind of bargain.

Pinned to its own king. That piece can't step off its line without exposing the king, so it's not leaving that line.

There was a pin to the king waiting in another move. Their piece would've been stuck there, since stepping off the line would expose the king. This move lets them off the hook.
Now that's a skewer! Go after the front piece, and once it gets out of the way, the one behind it is open for business. The prize is usually the one in the back.

Go after the defender first. Once it's gone, whatever it was guarding has lost that guard. Not elegant, just effective.
This leaves a defender where it can be captured. If the other side takes it, whatever it guards could lose its protection, so see what that defender is holding up.

The back rank turns into a cage. The king's own pieces block its escape, so its bodyguards are what trap it. Ugly for the defender, and it works.

The idea's promotion: march a pawn to the last rank and trade it in for a brand new piece. Cheapest upgrade in chess.

A stronger move would've had a pawn marching up to promote. That upgrade stays uncollected after this move.

Another move had a discovered attack lined up: shift one piece aside, and the one behind it gets its shot. This move never puts it to work.
Two threats, delivered by one move. That's a double attack, and one reply can't always cover both.

A stronger move had two attacks rolled into one. Nobody cashes in that double attack.
Lure the guard away from its post, and its old charge is free for the taking. Rude, but that is a deflection for you.
The other side now has a way to lure a defender off its job. It's called a deflection, and whatever the defender was minding could end up wide open.
There was a defender to lure away with another move. That deflection goes unused, and the defender keeps its job.
That piece had no defender, and this move takes it. Loose pieces are the first thing I look for, every time.
An undefended piece was there for another move to take, and this one walks right past it. Loose pieces first, clever ideas second.
A piece just got left with no defender, and the other side can walk up and take it. No fancy idea needed on their end.

There was a threat in the opponent's last move, and this move ignores it. Now a piece is just sitting there for them to take.
This capture looks like a deal until the recapture takes something worth more. Count the whole trade before you call it a bargain.
A knight or bishop finally leaves its starting square to go looking for work. Pieces sitting at home don't grab anything.
Another move would've gotten a minor piece off its starting square and working.
